paragraphs.text: Although copious volumes have been written on the subject, and many pilot projects initiated, the great, untapped energy of the oceans is still very largely untapped. The environmental arguments in favor of moving to a greater use of renewable energy, both on land and from the sea, are incontrovertible.

Tidal power, which exploits the twice-daily rise and fall of sea levels, is undoubtedly a valuable source of non-polluting, renewable energy, despite the limited number of potential sites around the world. But while the technological feasibility of tidal power has been proven, the main obstacle to increased use of the tides is that of initial construction costs. However, once established, a tidal power installation should have a lengthy operational lifetime, producing a supply of energy that is both inexhaustible and reliable, with less than 5% variation from year to year. The construction of the power plant involves building a major barrage across the mouth of a tidal river, which may be used simultaneously as a convenient highway or rail route, and can also serve to lessen the threat to vulnerable shorelines from storm waves and flooding. Although there are serious concerns about the effect of tidal power plants on feeding sites for birds and other animals, as well as on the passage of migratory fish, research has shown that the impacts depend greatly on local geography.

Of the thousands of small-scale tidal mills that generated power for hundreds of years in the pre-industrial age, only one remains – as a working museum in Totton, at the head of Southampton Water in southern England. The modern approach, however, is to think big. The high tide is temporarily held up in a great, enclosed bay behind the barrage, and then let out through a series of large turbines, generating electricity directly in much the same way as a hydroelectric plant on a river dam. In fact, the generators can be used in either direction, yielding power from flood and ebb tides. The first large-scale commercial scheme was the Rance barrage in Brittany, which has been feeding almost half a million kilowatts into the French national grid system daily since it opened in 1967. Fully worked-out designs and costings have often been drawn up for other tidal barrages, though yet comparatively few have been built.

Waves are another obvious and very visible source of energy. The power potential of an average wave per 1km of beach has been estimated at about 40 megawatts, but the means of harnessing this potential are largely in the research and development phase. A small-scale but commercial wave-power plant, known as OSPREY, was constructed off northern Scotland in 1995. Wave motion entered into a submerged chamber open at the base, forcing air upward through turbines. The 2-megawatt facility let the electricity generated to the shore some 300m away via an underwater cable. Unfortunately, the plant was soon damaged by waves and later destroyed by a storm – testimony to the power of the sea, as well as to our underdeveloped technology.

Still more elusive is the power bound up in ocean currents. Research has been carried out focusing on currents that are accelerated due to restricted flow through straits, around major headlands and peninsulas, or in the entrances to lochs and fjords. The calculations of the amount of potential energy that could be supplied by these hydroelectric hotspots are impressive. Pilot schemes have even been tested successfully utilizing both river flow (on the River Nile at Juba in 1980) and tidal flow (in the Kurashima Straits off Japan in 1988). Current power may well be a resource for the future, but it is of limited immediate interest.

Closer to reality is the idea that we could tap into the almost infinite supply of thermal energy in the oceans, and convert this directly to electricity. The principle of ocean thermal-energy conversion (OTEC) is to use the difference in temperature between warm surface water and cold deep water to drive a turbine and thus generate electricity. In tropical seas, surface waters at around 25-30°C overlie cold waters of 4-7°C at depths of 500-1,000m. The warm water can be used to vaporize an intermediate fuel, such as ammonia, which in turn serves to power the turbine. Cold water pumped up from the depths is put to use to condense the ammonia back into liquid form, so that the process can begin again. However, about 80% of the 50-kilowatt output is needed to pump the cold water up from the depths, leaving a net output of only 10-15 kilowatts – obviously a rather low level of efficiency. However, the potential is undoubtedly there. The Natural Energy Laboratory at Keahole Point in Hawaii has now developed an experimental 210-kilowatt OTEC plant. It has been calculated that the energy locked up in such thermal gradients within the oceans is nearly 10,000 times that available from tides and waves combined.
